title: The farewell sermon, in full
hook: at Arafah: your blood and property are sacred, treat women well, all of you are from Adam, and Adam from dust

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Christians of Najran prayed in the mosque, and the Prophet said: let them be. Your line was: guests in the mosque. Who did you welcome? Day seven hundred ninety-five.

The plain of Arafah, outside Mecca, on the day of the pilgrimage. A crowd in white. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is performing what Muslims call the farewell pilgrimage. Jabir ibn Abdullah, in Sahih Muslim, tells how he rides into the valley and speaks to the people. His first words tie three sacred things together: your blood and your property are sacred to you, as sacred as this day of yours, in this month of yours, in this city of yours. Today: the farewell sermon.
screen: `THE PLAIN OF ARAFAH.` → `HE SPEAKS TO THE PEOPLE.` → `AS SACRED AS THIS DAY.`

segments.voice: The sermon isn't kept in one single document. Its lines are spread across the hadith collections, each narrator remembering a part, and today we'll gather a few of them. Jabir's account keeps his words about women: be mindful of God in how you treat them, for you have taken them on a trust from God. The next day, the day of sacrifice at Mina, Sahih al-Bukhari reports him asking questions. What day is this? What month? What city? In Abu Bakrah's report, each time the crowd answers: Allah and His messenger know best. Then he tells them: your blood, your property and your honor are as sacred to one another as this day, in this month, in this city. He takes a sacred day, a sacred month and a sacred city, and lays them over every single person in front of him. And then the line in today's carry. In reports in the collections of Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi, which some readers gather into the sermon, he says that people are all children of Adam, and Adam was made from dust. No Arab has any merit over a non-Arab, and no non-Arab over an Arab, no light-skinned person over a dark-skinned one, nor the reverse, except by mindfulness of God. The Qur'an says something close in surah forty-nine: humankind was made into nations and tribes so that they might know one another, and the noblest in God's sight is the most mindful of Him. In Jabir's account, he asks what they will say when they are asked about him. They answer that he has conveyed the message. He raises his finger to the sky, points it toward the people, and says: O Allah, bear witness. And in Bukhari he tells those present to pass it on to those who are absent. That instruction is part of why you're hearing it now.
screen: `AS SACRED AS THIS DAY.` · `A TRUST FROM GOD.` · `CHILDREN OF ADAM, ADAM FROM DUST.` · `PASS IT TO THOSE ABSENT.` · then, large: `ALL FROM ADAM.`

segments.voice: The practice: read a translation of the sermon. If you can, find a translation of the farewell sermon from a reliable source, and use the bell's time to read slowly. If not, sit and hold just the three lines from today. Your blood and property are sacred. Treat women well, as a trust. All of you are from Adam, and Adam from dust. Let each one sit for a few breaths. Notice which line speaks most to your week. If you pray, you can ask Allah to help you live by it. The bell holds the time.
Arafah, the plain where, on his last pilgrimage, the Prophet declared each life and property sacred, and said all people are from Adam, and Adam from dust. Today's word.
Your line: all from Adam. Today, when you meet someone you'd usually rank above or below you, remember the dust you share. Day seven hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Muslims read the farewell sermon from the hadith collections, where its parts are spread across several narrations, and it is recited and taught at the time of the hajj and in Friday sermons.

fork.setup: you're in the crowd on the farewell pilgrimage. the Prophet asks: what day is this? what do you answer?
options: Allah and His messenger know best.
fork.reveal: that was their answer. then he told them: your blood, property and honor are as sacred as this day, in this month, in this city.

original.note: Arabic: 'the farewell pilgrimage', the name for the Prophet's last hajj.

trapdoor: what you thought: one famous speech.
what it means: a sacred day laid over every person, with care for women and the shared dust of Adam.
what a scholar hears: a sermon gathered from many narrations, in Bukhari, Muslim, Ahmad and others, each preserving parts.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 67; 1741 (Abu Bakrah's report of the sermon at Mina: what day is this; sacred as this day; let the present inform the absent)
Sahih Muslim 1218 (Jabir's account of the farewell pilgrimage: the sermon at Arafah, blood and property sacred, women a trust, O Allah bear witness)
Musnad Ahmad 23489; Jami' al-Tirmidhi 3270 (children of Adam, Adam from dust; no Arab over non-Arab)

notes: Audit (2026-10-01): Mina sermon was the day after Arafah (day of sacrifice), not 'a few days later'; fixed. The 'Allah and His messenger know best' answers are Abu Bakrah's report (Bukhari 67, 1741); in Ibn Abbas's report (1739) the people answer 'a sacred day', so the citation and myth now name Abu Bakrah.

Editor: the questions (what day, month, city?) and 'pass it on to the absent' come from the sermon at Mina in Bukhari, not Arafah; Arafah lines now credited to Jabir in Muslim (sacred blood and property, women, 'O Allah, bear witness'); the Adam-from-dust line framed as reports some readers gather into the sermon; fork no longer places the question at Arafah.
All hadith numbers given from memory; confirm, especially Ahmad 23489 and Tirmidhi 3270.
Qur'an 49:13 paraphrased; Pickthall not quoted because exact wording was not certain.
The 'no Arab over non-Arab' line is in Ahmad and is not in Bukhari or Muslim; confirm grading language.
Title says 'in full' but the script gathers selected lines and sends the listener to a full translation in the practice; confirm acceptable.
'Raises his finger' follows Jabir's report in Muslim (pointing to the sky and then to the people); confirm.
'Recited and taught at the time of the hajj and in Friday sermons' in howItsDone: confirm.
